title: The sacrifice
hook: an animal is sacrificed, and the meat shared

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jamarat, small stones and a takbir with each, and your line: reject the whisper. When the quiet nudge came back, did you manage one small no? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-four.

A rule about leftovers, and then a change to it. One Eid in Medina, Aisha reports, a group of poor families arrived from the desert. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told the people: keep the meat of your sacrifice for three days, and give away the rest. Later, people came to him unsure. Were they still bound by it? His answer: I only forbade it because of the families who had come. Now eat, store, and give. The rule had been shaped around hungry guests. Today, the sacrifice.
screen: `A RULE ABOUT LEFTOVERS.` → `FAMILIES ARRIVE HUNGRY.` → `NOW EAT, STORE, AND GIVE.`

segments.voice: Back at Mina, after the stoning, Jabir's account in Sahih Muslim says the Prophet went to the place of sacrifice and offered animals with his own hand. Then a piece from each was cooked, and he ate of the meat and drank of the broth. The one who offered it sat down and ate it. That's the first thing to notice. The sacrifice becomes a meal. Second, who else eats. Surah Al-Hajj tells those who sacrifice to eat of it and to feed two kinds of people: the one who is content and doesn't ask, and the one who does ask. Both the quiet poor and the poor who knock. Third, the line that turns the whole act around. The same surah says: "Their flesh and their blood reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him." The meat stays here, on earth, on plates. What goes up is something you can't weigh. Fourth, Aisha's story from the hook, in Sahih Muslim. A rule about storing meat was set because hungry families had come, and loosened when they hadn't. The sacrifice keeps looking at who is at the door. And it isn't only for pilgrims. At Eid al-Adha, Muslims at home who are able offer an animal too, and remember Ibrahim, whose story of a ransomed son is told in Surah As-Saffat. So the same day, at Mina and far from it, there's blood, then a fire, then a pot, then a knock, then a plate passed across a table.
screen: `HE ATE OF THE MEAT.` · `THE CONTENT AND THE ONE WHO ASKS.` · `THE DEVOTION REACHES HIM.` · `A RULE SHAPED BY HUNGRY GUESTS.` · then, large: `THEIR FLESH AND THEIR BLOOD REACH NOT ALLAH.`

segments.voice: The practice: share a meal, starting in your head. Settle, and breathe. Think of the food you'll eat in the next day or two. Then think of who could eat some of it with you. Someone who'd never ask. A neighbor, an older relative, a coworker eating alone. Or someone who would ask, if they knew they could. Pick one. Picture handing them the plate. If you pray, you can thank God for the food before you share it. If you don't, just hold the picture until it feels like a plan. The bell holds the time.
The sacrifice. An animal offered in God's name on the day of sacrifice, its meat eaten and shared, and only the devotion reaching God. Today's word.

Your line: shared meat. This week took you from Zamzam, through Safa and Marwa, Mina, Arafah and Muzdalifah, to the stones and the sacrifice. Today, share one meal or one dish with someone. Tomorrow: shaving or trimming. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Pilgrims offer an animal at Mina after the stoning, and Muslims at home who are able offer one at Eid al-Adha; the meat is eaten by the household and shared with friends and with people in need.

pairs: he ate of the meat and drank the broth
feed the content and the one who asks

myth: the Qur'an says the flesh and blood of the sacrifice reach God
it says the reverse: their flesh and blood reach not Allah, but the devotion does.
the Prophet once limited storing the meat because hungry families had arrived
Aisha reports it, and later he said: now eat, store, and give.
the meat is only for people who ask for it
Surah Al-Hajj names the content who don't ask, and those who do.

fork.setup: some time after the rule about storing meat. you ask the Prophet whether you still have to give away whatever is left after three days. what does he say?
options: it was because of the hungry families. now eat, store, and give.
fork.reveal: he explains the rule was for the families who had come, and loosens it: eat, store, and give in charity.

original.note: the pilgrim's offering at Mina; at home, the Eid sacrifice is called udhiyah.

trapdoor: what you thought: an animal killed as an offering sent up to God.
what it means: an animal sacrificed in God's name, its meat eaten and shared with the content and the one who asks.
what a scholar hears: 22:37 — the flesh and blood don't reach God; the devotion does.

sources.quoted: Their flesh and their blood reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him.

notes: Muslim 1218 (Jabir): sacrifice by his own hand, the rest given to Ali, a piece from each cooked, he ate the meat and drank the broth. The count of animals is deliberately left out. Confirm.
Muslim 1971 (Aisha): the 'daffah' of Bedouin families, the three-day limit, and its lifting the next year. Confirm number and summary.
Pickthall 22:37 wording: verify exactly before release.
22:36: 'the one who is content and the one who asks' paraphrases al-qani' and al-mu'tarr; commentators differ on the exact sense. Confirm.
Week-end look-back (days 1128–1134) placed in the carry.
Practice invites thanks 'if you pray'; no new prayer written.

Editor: 'the next year' (hook, myth, fork) changed to 'later', since Aisha's wording in Muslim 1971 gives no year (the 'next year' detail belongs to Salamah ibn al-Akwa's report, Bukhari 5569); cut 'isn't burned up or sent away', which read as an implied contrast with other traditions' offerings.
